{{short description|British statistician and demographer}}
{{distinguish|C. Jean Thompson}}
'''Jean Helen Thompson''' {{post-nominals|CBE}} (2 December 1926 – 28 December 1992) was a British [[statistics|statistician]] and [[demography|demographer]] who became chief statistician in the [[Office of Population Censuses and Surveys]].{{r|ind|jrss}}

Thompson earned a degree in statistics at [[University College London]], and began working for the [[Government Statistical Service]] in 1950. After moving through several other bureaus, she came to the [[General Register Office]], the predecessor organisation to the Office of Population Censuses and Surveys, as its chief statistician in 1967.{{r|jrss}} She also represented the UK on the [[United Nations Commission on Population and Development]].{{r|ind}} She retired in 1986.{{r|jrss}}

At the General Register Office, Thompson's main statistical concerns involved birth rates and immigration. However, she failed to foresee the end of the [[baby boom]] in the late 1960s and early 1970s.{{r|jrss}} In the late 1970s, when Labour politician [[Richard Crossman]]'s diaries were published posthumously, she was forced to sue the publisher for libel, for including claims that she was a member of a "Fascist nest" who had falsified statistics about ethnic minorities in Britain. The publishers could present no evidence that this was so, and were forced to apologise in court.{{r|ind|jrss}}<!-- The Independent's version of the story, that Crossman's undead body was brought to court and forced to apologise from beyond the grave, is likely apocryphal. -->

Thompson also served a term as president of the [[British Society for Population Studies]]. She was awarded the CBE on her retirement, "in recognition of her contributions both to the public service and to population studies".{{r|ind|jrss}}
